origins.section: An Override Is One More Rule, and Every Rule a Planner Can Change Sits Behind a Literal
Overrides Have a Price, and a Clash Names Its Rules
Six Tests: Three Overrides, Two Clashes, One Data Check

gates.says: all 3 of this quiz's answerable readings held and each was taken over the question as it stands

recorded.prompt:q-hard: Read the whole lesson page, then this question. Using only what the page states, which option does the page decide is correct? Quote or cite the deciding passage.
recorded.outcome:q-hard: The hard facts stay hard: windows, crews' weeks off, one trim per crew at a time. They are physics, not decisions; an explanation that says "or let K1 work two circuits at once" is not one a planner can act on.
recorded.prompt:q-clash: Read the whole lesson page, then this question. Using only what the page states, which option does the page decide is correct? Quote or cite the deciding passage.
recorded.outcome:q-clash: Of the season's five changeable rules (two musts, the budget and these two pins), the other three are not mentioned, because they are not part of the clash.
recorded.prompt:q-innocent: Read the whole lesson page, then this question. Using only what the page states, which option does the page decide is correct? Quote or cite the deciding passage.
recorded.outcome:q-innocent: Override 1 (force C) is there on purpose: it is a rule the explanation must *leave out*. Without it, an explanation that listed every override would pass.
